analysis.one_liner: Makes oil companies pay the full cost of offshore oil spills, ending a $75 million liability cap.
analysis.headline: The Senate never voted on the bill; it sat in the Environment and Public Works Committee from January 2011 until the 112th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would remove the $75 million cap on what the company responsible for an offshore oil spill must pay for cleanup and damages. Under current law, once costs pass $75 million, the extra burden falls on a federal oil-spill trust fund and ultimately taxpayers. The bill would have taken effect retroactively to April 15, 2010, just before the Deepwater Horizon spill.
analysis.who_benefits: Coastal residents, fishing businesses, and tourism economies that suffer damage from oil spills, because the company that caused the spill would have to pay all cleanup and damage costs rather than stop at $75 million. Taxpayers also benefit, because they would no longer backstop spill costs above the cap through the federal trust fund.

how_it_helps.text: Removes the $75 million liability cap so the responsible party pays the total of all removal costs and damages for each offshore spill, not just the first $75 million.
Keeps taxpayers from absorbing spill costs above the cap, which is the practical effect of the current cap.
Takes effect on April 15, 2010, so it would apply to spills from that date forward, including the Deepwater Horizon disaster of April 20, 2010.

analysis.who_pays: Oil and gas companies operating offshore facilities, which would face unlimited liability for any spill they cause. Some of that cost could be passed through to consumers in the form of higher fuel prices, and the added legal risk could make it harder for smaller drilling companies to operate.

drawbacks.text: Unlimited liability raises the cost and risk of offshore drilling, and energy companies argue those costs can flow to consumers through higher prices at the pump.
The bill applies retroactively to April 15, 2010, before it was enacted, which raises fairness concerns about changing legal rules after the fact.
Opponents also argue that uncapped liability could push drilling to operators with less ability to pay, since the cap gives some assurance that a responsible party can actually cover a spill.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is straightforward: whoever causes a spill pays for all of it, and taxpayers are not left covering the difference. The main cost is uncertainty for the offshore drilling industry and possible price pass-through to consumers. On balance, the bill shifts a real, existing cost burden from the public back onto the companies that create the risk, which is why the oil industry opposed it.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee, which never acted on it, so it died there when the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Robert Menendez introduced the bill on January 27, 2011, in the aftermath of the 2010 Deepwater Horizon spill, with eight Democratic cosponsors and no Republican support on the record.
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Environment and Public Works the same day.
No further action ever appears in the record: no committee markup, no floor debate, no vote, through the end of the 112th Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Offshore oil producers are better off because the bill died: the $75 million liability cap stays in place, and spill costs above that line continue to fall on the federal trust fund and taxpayers rather than on the industry.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Oil companies kept the liability cap

for.name: Sen. Robert Menendez
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to lift the $75 million offshore spill liability cap.

for.name: 8 Democratic cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Senate Republican cosponsored it.

against.name: Senate Environment and Public Works Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Sen. Barbara Boxer (D-CA)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on January 27, 2011 and never brought it to a markup or sent it to the floor; no further action appears in the record for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Oil and gas industry
against.role: Companies and trade groups affected by offshore spill liability
against.what_they_did: Opposed lifting the liability cap after the Deepwater Horizon spill, arguing unlimited liability would raise drilling costs and threaten domestic energy production.

sides.party_line_note: All nine senators on record supporting the bill were Democrats, and no Republican action on it appears in the record; the bill never reached a vote, so no roll-call breakdown exists.

industries.note: The bill would make them pay every dollar of cleanup and damages from a spill instead of stopping at $75 million. Their interest in keeping the cap runs against the public's, since the cap shifts spill costs above $75 million onto the federal trust fund and taxpayers.

industries.industry: Commercial fishing and coastal tourism businesses
industries.note: Full recovery of spill damages would better compensate the businesses that lose the most when coastal waters are fouled. Their interest runs alongside coastal residents' and taxpayers'.
